lead: An array shapes its pattern by changing element amplitudes or phases. Amplitude tapering trades main-beam width against sidelobes: binomial coefficients remove sidelobes, Chebyshev coefficients give the narrowest beam for a stated sidelobe level. A constant phase step steers the beam without moving the array. Radar, satellite links and 5G base stations use these trades.
prereq: You need: the array factor and broadside/end-fire phasing from Chapter 3.2.

blocks.text: Take N equally spaced elements on a line, spacing d metres, real amplitudes an and progressive phase α radians per element. Measure θ from broadside. The array factor sums element contributions. The element pattern multiplies it; see Chapter 3.1.
AF(θ) = Σ<sub>n=0</sub><sup>N−1</sup> a<sub>n</sub> e<sup>j n ψ</sup>,  ψ = βd sinθ + α
blocks.where: AF(θ) is the array factor at angle θ; N is the number of elements; a<sub>n</sub> is the amplitude of element n; ψ is the total electrical phase step between adjacent elements; β = 2π/λ is the phase constant in rad/m; d is the element spacing in m; θ is measured from broadside; α is the progressive phase shift in rad.

blocks.text: A uniform array sets a<sub>n</sub> = 1. Its first sidelobe is about −13 dB. Tapering makes edge elements smaller than centre elements; the main beam widens and sidelobes fall. Binomial taper uses Pascal-triangle coefficients: 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1.

blocks.where: C(N−1,n) is the binomial coefficient, read as (N−1) choose n. For N = 4 the amplitudes are 1, 3, 3, 1.

blocks.text: With d = λ/2 and α = 0, the binomial array factor is proportional to |cos(ψ/2)|<sup>N−1</sup>, ψ = βd sinθ. In −π ≤ ψ ≤ π it peaks once at ψ = 0, so no sidelobes. The cost is a wide main beam and low aperture efficiency. For d > λ/2 the visible range grows and this property fails.

Chebyshev (Dolph-Chebyshev) sets all sidelobes to one chosen level. For voltage ratio R, the design parameter is x<sub>0</sub>. Coefficients come from a Chebyshev polynomial mapped into visible space. For given N and sidelobe level, this gives minimum main-beam width. Coefficients need tables or a computer.
x<sub>0</sub> = cosh( (1/(N−1)) cosh<sup>−1</sup> R ),  SLL<sub>dB</sub> = −20 log<sub>10</sub> R
blocks.where: R is main-lobe to sidelobe voltage ratio, R > 1; x<sub>0</sub> is the Chebyshev design parameter; SLL<sub>dB</sub> is sidelobe level relative to the main lobe in dB, negative. A −20 dB sidelobe means R = 10.

sections.h3: Phased array: steering with a phase step

blocks.text: Keep amplitudes fixed and change only α. The main beam sits where ψ = 0, because every element then adds in phase. Rearranging ψ = βd sinθ + α = 0 gives the steering law. A negative α steers to positive θ, and a positive α steers to negative θ.

blocks.where: θ<sub>0</sub> is the main-beam angle from broadside in rad; α is the progressive phase shift in rad; β = 2π/λ in rad/m; d is the spacing in m. For d = λ/2, βd = π, so α = −π sinθ<sub>0</sub>.

blocks.text: A phased array uses one phase shifter per element after a power divider. The beam can jump to a new angle in microseconds because nothing mechanical moves. Phase-shifter circuits are covered in Unit 4, Microwave Components, Devices and Measurements. The same array can also use an amplitude taper, so steering and sidelobe control are separate adjustments.

Large element spacing creates grating lobes: extra directions where ψ = ±2πm also gives a maximum. For a beam steered to θ<sub>0</sub>, the first grating lobe stays outside visible space when d/λ is small enough. The usual choice d = λ/2 avoids grating lobes for every scan angle of a linear array.

blocks.where: d is the element spacing in m; λ is the free-space wavelength in m; θ<sub>0</sub> is the scan angle from broadside. At broadside this allows d ≤ λ; at endfire it allows d ≤ λ/2.

blocks.text: Fixed phase shifters make the beam angle depend on frequency. This is beam squint. At design frequency f<sub>0</sub>, α is set for θ<sub>0</sub>. At another frequency f, β changes but α stays fixed, so the beam moves. A higher frequency makes |sinθ<sub>0</sub>| smaller, so the beam moves toward broadside. Wideband systems use true-time-delay units or digital beamforming to reduce squint.

blocks.where: f is frequency in Hz; c is the speed of light in m/s; α is the fixed progressive phase in rad; d is spacing in m; θ<sub>0</sub>(f) is the beam angle at frequency f.

sections.h3: Choosing a taper and a steering method

blocks.text: Use the taper to meet a sidelobe specification and the phase to meet a scan requirement. A binomial array suits a short array that must avoid sidelobes, such as a simple low-interference link. A Chebyshev array suits radar or point-to-point links where a strong jammer or nearby transmitter must be rejected while keeping a narrow beam. A phased array suits any system that must scan quickly: radar, satellite user terminals and 5G base stations.

figure.caption: Four-element linear phased array set for θ₀ = 30° with d = λ/2. The divider feeds phase shifters 0°, −90°, −180°, −270°, so the beam steers from broadside.

spec.aria: Four-element phased array: a power divider feeds phase shifters set to 0°, −90°, −180° and −270°, steering the beam to 30° from broadside.

examples.question: A 4-element linear phased array has element spacing d = λ/2 and equal amplitudes. It must steer its main beam to θ₀ = 30° from broadside. Find the progressive phase shift α between adjacent elements and list the phase of each element.
steps: Identify the data: N = 4, d = λ/2, θ₀ = 30°, equal amplitudes.
Compute βd. β = 2π/λ, so βd = (2π/λ)(λ/2) = π rad.
Use the steering law sinθ₀ = −α/(βd). Rearrange: α = −βd sinθ₀.
Element n has phase nα for n = 0, 1, 2, 3. The phases are 0°, −90°, −180° and −270°.
examples.answer: The progressive phase shift is α = −π/2 rad = −90° per element, and the element phases are 0°, −90°, −180° and −270°.
examples.check:
import math
beta_d = math.pi
theta0_deg = 30.0
alpha_rad = -beta_d * math.sin(math.radians(theta0_deg))
alpha_deg = math.degrees(alpha_rad)
phases = [0.0, alpha_deg, 2.0 * alpha_deg, 3.0 * alpha_deg]
print(alpha_rad)
print(alpha_deg)
for p in phases:
    print(p)

traps: Chebyshev does not remove sidelobes; it sets them all to a chosen level, such as −20 dB. Binomial removes sidelobes, only for d ≤ λ/2.
With θ from broadside, use α = −βd sinθ₀. Using cosθ₀ steers wrongly. If θ is from the array axis, sine and cosine swap.
A binomial array with d > λ/2 gains extra lobes because the visible ψ range extends past ±π.
Sidelobe dB has a sign. A −20 dB sidelobe gives voltage ratio R = 10, not 0.01. Use R = 10<sup>−SLL<sub>dB</sub>/20</sup>.
Grating lobes are extra main beams from large spacing, not sidelobes. Check d/λ ≤ 1/(1 + |sinθ₀|) before blaming the taper.

quiz.q: What does the progressive phase α represent in an N-element linear array?
quiz.a: It is the phase added per element relative to the previous element, in radians. Element n has total phase nα relative to element 0.

quiz.q: Why does a binomial array have no sidelobes when d = λ/2 and α = 0?
quiz.a: Its array factor is proportional to |cos(ψ/2)|<sup>N−1</sup> with ψ = βd sinθ. For d = λ/2 the visible range is −π ≤ ψ ≤ π. In that range |cos(ψ/2)| falls from 1 at ψ = 0 to 0 at ψ = ±π without a second peak, so there is no sidelobe.

quiz.q: A 4-element array with d = λ/2 must steer to θ₀ = −20° from broadside. Find α and the four element phases.
A radar must reject a strong sidelobe jammer. Compare a binomial taper and a Chebyshev taper for this job.
quiz.a: Chebyshev sets every sidelobe to a chosen low level and gives the narrowest main beam for that level, so it rejects the jammer while keeping angular resolution. Binomial removes sidelobes but makes the main beam much wider, so resolution and gain fall.

quiz.q: State the condition for no grating lobe when a linear array is steered to θ₀.
quiz.a: d/λ ≤ 1/(1 + |sinθ₀|). At broadside this allows d ≤ λ; at endfire it allows d ≤ λ/2.

quiz.q: A phased array is designed at 10 GHz with fixed phase shifters for θ₀ = 40°. At 12 GHz, does the beam move toward broadside or toward endfire? Use the squint formula.
quiz.a: For fixed α, sinθ₀(f) = −αc/(2πfd), so |sinθ₀| ∝ 1/f. At 10 GHz, sin 40° = 0.643. At 12 GHz, sinθ₀ = 0.643 × 10/12 = 0.536, so θ₀ ≈ 32.4°. The beam moves toward broadside.

quiz.q: A 4-element array with d = λ/2 uses phase steps 0°, −90°, −180° and −270°. Find θ₀.
quiz.a: α = −90° = −π/2 rad. sinθ₀ = −α/(βd) = −(−π/2)/π = 0.5. Therefore θ₀ = 30° from broadside.

quiz.q: Why is phase steering faster than mechanical rotation?
quiz.a: There is no moving mass. An electronic phase shifter changes its phase in microseconds, so the beam can switch angle almost instantly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Active electronically scanned arrays put a phase shifter and amplifier behind every element, and digital beamforming replaces some phase shifters with per-element digital weights. Wideband and satellite systems use true-time-delay units to remove beam squint. 5G massive MIMO uses linear and planar phased arrays at millimetre waves. Search terms: AESA, true-time-delay beamforming, massive MIMO beam steering, Dolph-Chebyshev synthesis.
